An AI model asked to audit the trace of another agent refused to do so, because the trace described screenshots to be taken silently every few seconds. When the word silently was removed, the audit went ahead. The finding sits in a study released in October 2026 by researchers at Purdue University, which tested a 2 stage monitor on OpenAgentSafety, a public benchmark of workplace tasks in which agents are pressed by simulated colleagues to take unsafe actions. Rules select which pending actions are sent to an AI auditor, and the auditor reads the preceding trace before the action is executed. The provider's safety guardrails rejected 15 of 347 audit requests, 14 of them on unsafe runs. The authors treated each refusal as a detection. 14 of the 59 detections made by the selective monitor rested on nothing but a refusal, and without them its detection rate would fall from 72.8% to 55.6% or below. A safety trained auditor may decline to read the evidence it was deployed to examine, and the traces with the highest chance of refusal are the ones that carry the most risk. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

## ABSTRACT

This paper advances a way of thinking the body in human geography through gestures, their capacity to refuse inoperatively and their relation to unconscious processes. Extending insights from non-representational and embodied approaches to gestures in the field, it treats gestures as a distinct analytic and develops the concept of ‘inoperative refusal’ to account for how unconscious, corporeal practices interrupt axes of bodily discipline and surveillance without becoming intentional or representational forms of resistance. Through gestures, the body refuses. Drawing on a psychoanalytic reading of gestures via the work of Donald Winnicott, the paper reclaims the unconscious for the body and situates queer gestures as instances of the inoperative refusal. To examine how such refusal might operate collectively, I place it in dialogue with Herbert Marcuse's ‘Great Refusal’ (1955) and Maurice Blanchot's ‘pure means’ refusal (2010), which offer resources for thinking refusal towards non-programmatic forms of collective action. I aim to show how thinking about gestures as such may lead us to an alternative politics of refusal. Recent scholarship in human geography has engaged ‘refusal’ as a concept for understanding how marginalised subjects and communities set limits on participation in, and incorporation by, dominant political and epistemic frameworks. This engagement draws on foundational interventions by Simpson (2007, 2014, 2017) and TallBear (2013), whose work on Indigenous sovereignty theorises refusal as a practice of withholding recognition and delimiting the terms of engagement with settler states, and by Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang, who frame refusal as a stance against extractive research logics (2014). Carole McGranahan further consolidates this approach by emphasising how refusal is generative rather than simply oppositional (2016). Human geographers have extended these insights into analyses of borders, migration and colonial power, as well as into methodological debates about fieldwork and the ethics of access, where refusal is understood as enacted through withholding, non-participation and limits on knowledge production (Guasco 2022; Jones 2012; Meier 2023; Wright 2018). Notably, for the emergence of negative geographies, Dekeyser and Jellis turn to refusal as a means of ‘staying with the tension’ and not simply reversing affirmationism to find a space for negative geographies (2021).

At the same time, there remains some ambiguity regarding the degree to which refusal may be understood as a conscious and strategic decision. Accounts grounded in Indigenous politics often emphasise refusal as an intentional act: a deliberate withholding, disengagement or non-compliance that asserts sovereignty and sets limits on recognition. Recent work in human geography suggests a different but complementary approach. Analyses of encounters within politically constrained environments indicate that what is interpreted as refusal can emerge through situated, relational and sometimes tacit practices. Jones (2012) follows the unauthorised border-crossing into India by a 62-year-old woman from Bangladesh, where she works as a servant for a wealthy family, to spend a month visiting her son and grandson. Jones's concept of ‘spaces of refusal’ shows how everyday practices of evasion and disregard can refuse to abide by the state's binary territorial and identity categories, even when they do not take the form of overt political resistance. Accordingly, refusal may involve partial disengagement, strategic ambiguity or forms of non-participation that are not always framed by participants themselves as deliberate acts. From this perspective, refusal may be better understood as a situated practice that is not reducible to conscious, intentional decision-making, including more ambiguous forms of disengagement under conditions of constraint. Following this thread of ambiguity, recent studies attending to gestures in human geography are concerned with how gestures articulate a certain politics of refusal by Black queer women in American gentrifying neighbourhoods (Adeyemi 2019; Seitz and Proudfoot 2021), by Palestinian people expressing humour and laughter in the heavily surveilled environment of border control security (Bhungalia 2020), and by people in Delhi taking over unfinished urban development projects ‘through practices of squatting and repair’ (Boudreau 2023; Simone et al. 2023).

This paper contributes to this thread of scholarship tracing the ambiguity of refusal through a theorisation of gestures as the medium through which the body goes on strike—unlike a conventional labour strike because it operates without intentionality—or, in other words, its inoperative refusal. To find one of the most sustained engagements with gestures and the connection between the psyche and the body, I will now turn to psychoanalysis and the writing of Winnicott. It is in this literature that I will argue for a reclaiming of the unconscious for the body via gestures.

## Scope of Review

This review is concerned with whether the Department was justified, under section 15(1)(a) in refusing to release further records relevant to parts 1-3, 5-10, 17, 18 (other than records held by the Inspectorate Unit) and 19-23 of his request. Furthermore, the applicant sought a review of the Department’s decision to refuse, in full or in part, certain records listed in the Schedule provided by the Teacher/SNA Terms and Conditions Unit, specifically records 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, 20, 30 and 107, under various exemptions. The review will consider whether the Department was justified in refusing these records.

It is important to note at this point that the review will not consider records falling within the scope of the request that are held or potentially held by the Inspectorate Unit. The previous decision by this Office (OIC-134268-W5V8R7) already addressed this.

In his application for review, the applicant stated that some of the records released contained handwritten notes that he was unable to decipher (12, 22, 23, 27, 33, 34, 36, 89 and 11), and that some of the records were in light print and difficult to read (2 and 30). It is open to the applicant to engage with the Department and to see if it is possible for a transcript or clearer copy of the records to be provided. This will not form part of the review.

## Preliminary Matters

Before I address the substantive issues arising, I wish to address some preliminary matters.

In communication with this Office in response to the update I sent to him on 24 September 2024, including the details of searches carried out, the applicant noted that the Department did not explicitly reference section 15(1)(a) in the Schedule of Records issued to him. Firstly, I note that the purpose of a Schedule of Records is to list the relevant records that have been found by an FOI body and to set out its decision in respect of each record, and the relevant exemption if that record has been refused. It therefore does not follow that the Schedule would include records that have not been found. Secondly, whether explicitly stated or not, if it is a requester’s position that further records exist while it is the FOI body’s position that they do not, this is effectively a refusal to release records under section 15(1)(a).
I believe this to go beyond the taking of reasonable steps, which will be examined in more detail under section 15(1)(a) below. The applicant is familiar with his own case, and it was open to him to point to records that he believed to be missing and to make reference to a specific part of his request; indeed, he did this in respect of specific records falling within parts 1 and 8 of the request. I do not believe that the applicant has been disadvantaged by the approach taken and will proceed with the review on the substantive matters.

In submissions, the applicant said that as the records concerned his role as a primary school teacher and were about him and his employment, he believed that “the threshold for refusal of records is far higher”. He referred to a reference to case 98017 in the Guidance Note on section 15(1)(c) as support for this. The applicant also highlighted the anxiety and stress that he said the delay in bringing his FOI request to a conclusion has caused him. While it is of course regrettable that it has taken so long, it is important to note that section 13(4) of the Act provides that in deciding whether to grant or refuse a request, any reason that the requester gives for the request shall be disregarded. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# How to remove a Google review (fake or defamatory): doctors, hotels, restaurants, e-commerce…

The law is not powerless against fake online reviews such as those posted on Google: disparagement, defamation, misleading commercial practice, legal obligations of platforms. You still need to choose the right characterisation, the right target and the right timing. In this article we explain, step by step, how to act effectively.

§In brief

## How to remove a fake or defamatory Google review ?

First move: report the review from the establishment's Google Maps listing, through the review menu then "Report review", in a few clicks. Google removes content that breaches its policies, but rejects most reports about fake or defamatory reviews. Where reporting fails, the legal route takes over: a reasoned formal notice to the platform, action against the author and compensation for the harm.

INFLUXIO Expertise

A business discovers on its Google Business Profile a series of one-star reviews signed by people who have never been its customers. The question is always the same: how do you remove a fake Google review, identify its author and obtain compensation?

The answer is yes, a fake Google review can be removed, provided three mistakes are avoided: believing that a simple report to Google will be enough, choosing the wrong legal characterisation between disparagement and defamation, and letting time slip by, since some actions are time-barred after three months.

## Fake review, negative review or defamatory review: how to characterise a disputed Google review?

An online review is a consumer's opinion about their experience (Article D111-9 of the French Consumer Code). One important point: that experience counts even without a purchase. A prospect disappointed by a phone call or an in-store visit gives a genuine review, even without paying anything.

A fake Google review is something else: its author had no real experience with the business. It is the paid review, the coordinated fraudulent review campaign, the message from a competitor, a former employee or an adversary posing as a customer. Medical and paramedical professionals, doctors, surgeons, dentists, physiotherapists, vets, clinics and group practices, are among the most exposed targets, since their Google listing largely drives new appointment bookings.

A Google review is not fake because it is harsh: it is fake when its author never had the slightest experience with the business.

Instead, we ask: What else can childhood studies do when childhood is released from its temporal constraints? If tracing “the child” presupposes a stable foundation, what new forms of thought, relation, or resistance emerge when tracing is refused? Put another way, what escapes us when temporality is preserved as the essence of childhood?

Exploring possibilities outside a stable, traceable child subject, in this special issue, we consider, as Rachel Rosen (2017) does, how our conceptions of time have “bearing on the ways in which we frame research problems and on the types of analysis we produce” (p. 378). We see this special issue contributing to current debates at this junction. We are indebted to those who have already written on children and temporalities, pushing childhood studies beyond its familiar margins. Because of these conversations, the field is in an exciting temporal landscape, exploring questions of time and its effects, even though these critical inquiries may undermine the foundation of the field. But this pushing also shows that we do not need linear time to justify childhood as a valid field of inquiry. We do not need to rely on an essence of childhood to ground political claims as compelling possibilities for theorizing childhood emerge through temporalities not tethered to a stable, traceable child subject. Examples include memory and affect (Dyer & Mecija, this issue), duration (Pomerantz, 2024), diffraction (Sheppard, this issue), waiting and longing (Jones, this issue), hope (Millei, 2021), and lingering (Pacini-Ketchabaw & MacAlpine, this issue), among others. Our contributors write about childhood using many of these non-sequential temporalities, noting that linear time preserves a certain kind of child while barring other kinds who may or may not be contained by flesh or by legal-, rights-, and age-based criteria.

Cosenza scaffolds his thesis through a reconstruction of the conceptual “flow” running through Lacan’s sparse, often elliptical remarks on anorexia across the span of his teaching. This effort allows for the articulation of the logic underlying the symptom’s core performative gesture, and for a mapping of the structural coordinates that this refusal responds to. The anorexic’s radical “no” is thus traced through four distinct positions Lacan assumed throughout the evolution of his thought. In the process, what emerges is not only a reading of anorexia but also an implicit masterclass in Lacan’s theoretical development, curated around the traces of a single signifier.

Cosenza takes off with Lacan’s earliest comments in “The Family Complexes” from 1938, where—still under Kleinian influence—the young Lacan conceives of anorexia as a refusal of weaning, a resistance to separating from the maternal rapport. This position, Cosenza notes, Lacan later abandons, only to return to it much later in his teaching, but reframed: not as a clinging to the maternal imago, but as a drive toward unity with the One—the omnipotent, seamless rapport that retains the trace of the maternal, is now articulated through Lacan’s critique of the discourse of the markets and its emblematic rejection of lack. Refusal, in Cosenza, amounts to a logic that operates on many levels: as metaphor, as defense, as an attempt for separation, and as pure jouissance of the body in its control over the drive, which is a symptomatic ideal of our times. Through the four functions of refusal Cosenza demonstrates how the positivity of the solution is enacted, laying the ground for a clinic that not only addresses the dialectical aspects of the symptom but fully engages with a new clinical horizon: a clinic of the Real, of jouissance, of the drive-body.

Refusal, in Cosenza’s formulation, is far more than oppositional behavior or the byproduct of ego weakness. It is a complex, composite formation in which negativism and compliance are intricately grafted together—a singular strategy the anorexic subject deploys to navigate massive, unsolvable contradictions. She both defies and submits in her proclivity for complacency, revealing a psychic geography fractured between two poles: an absent, blind to singularity, evacuated Other and an excessively demanding, jouissance-driven, ever-engulfing Other.
